title: Why You Need To Give Frequent Reminders The First Week Of School
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin distinguishes between reminders given after misbehavior begins, which he considers a mistake that undermines accountability, and reminders given proactively before misbehavior has a chance to occur, which he strongly recommends especially during the first week of school. He outlines three benefits of pre-misbehavior reminders: they largely eliminate misbehavior by removing excuses and forgetfulness, they help establish early success and good habits that snowball through the year, and they make consequences easier and more consistent to enforce because students can no longer claim confusion. As students demonstrate mastery of routines over time, the frequency of reminders should taper off, gradually shifting more responsibility onto the class.
points: Distinguishes harmful post-misbehavior reminders (a veiled threat that replaces accountability) from beneficial pre-misbehavior reminders.
Pre-misbehavior reminders during the first week largely eliminate common misbehaviors by removing excuses and forgetfulness.
Early proactive reminders help 'groove success,' since early wins compound and shape the trajectory of the whole year.
Removing students' ability to claim confusion makes enforcing consequences easier and more consistent.
As students prove mastery of routines, reminders should be phased out and responsibility gradually shifted to students.
quotes: In fact, they’re examples of what you should never do —first week of school or not—because they’re reminders given after misbehavior has already begun.
The reason is that post-misbehavior reminders replace true accountability. They’re given instead of enforcing a consequence.
This very effectively makes misbehavior a hard choice for students rather than an impulsive act.
When you give pre-misbehavior reminders, you remove the awkwardness of enforcing consequences.
Your trust in them and their abilities will grow, and you’ll gradually shift more and more responsibility over to them with less input from you.
Before I say ‘go,’ remember to line up quietly and keep your hands to yourself.
